---
title: "RStudio projects and cloning a repository"
subtitle: "Guide 3 of 4 · do this once per repository"
---

## What a project is, and why it matters

An RStudio **project** is a folder with an `.Rproj` file in it. That one file
changes how RStudio behaves in three ways that save you hours:

- **The working directory is the project folder.** Every file path in your code
  can be written relative to the project, so `read_csv("data/survey.csv")` works
  on your laptop, on a lab machine, and on your grader's computer. You never
  need `setwd()` again, and you should never use it.
- **Each project gets its own session.** Open two projects and you get two
  separate R sessions, with their own environments and command histories. Work
  on one analysis does not leak into another.
- **RStudio shows you the Git tab.** Version control only appears when the
  folder RStudio has open is a Git repository *and* an RStudio project.

The rule that follows from this: **always open your work by opening the project,
never by opening a single `.R` or `.qmd` file from your file browser.** Opening a
loose file gives you the editor without the working directory, without the Git
tab, and with paths that break.

## Keep your projects in one folder

Before you clone anything, decide where projects live and stick to it. One
folder in your home directory, holding one subfolder per project:

```
~/gph2182/
  weekly-exercise-01-yourusername/
  weekly-exercise-02-yourusername/
  in-class-exercises-yourusername/
```

This matters more than it sounds. Over a semester you accumulate a dozen
repositories, and if they are scattered across Desktop, Downloads, and a
half-synced cloud folder, you will lose one. With a single parent folder,
switching between them is **File > Recent Projects**.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Cloud-synced folders

Putting Git repositories inside Dropbox, OneDrive, iCloud Drive, or Google Drive
causes real trouble: the sync client and Git both try to manage the same files
and can corrupt the repository's internal state. Git is already your backup, and
GitHub is already your cloud copy. Use a plain local folder.
:::

## Situation A: the repository already exists on GitHub

This is the common case: someone has given you a URL, or you accepted an
assignment and GitHub created a repository for you. You want a local copy, which
is called **cloning**.

Copy the repository URL first. On the repository's GitHub page, click the green
**Code** button and copy the HTTPS URL. It looks like
`https://github.com/owner/repository-name.git`. The URL in your browser's
address bar works too.

Then use either route below.

### Route 1: the RStudio menu

1. **File > New Project > Version Control > Git**
2. Paste the URL into **Repository URL**. The project directory name fills in by
   itself; leave it.
3. Set **Create project as subdirectory of** to your projects folder
   (`~/gph2182`, or wherever you chose above).
4. Click **Create Project**.

RStudio downloads the repository and opens it as a project.

### Route 2: one line in the Console

Faster once you are comfortable, and it needs no clicking:

```r
dir.create("~/gph2182", showWarnings = FALSE)
usethis::create_from_github("owner/repository-name", destdir = "~/gph2182")
```

`owner/repository-name` is the last two segments of the repository URL. The
first line creates the parent folder if it does not exist yet, which matters
because `create_from_github()` fails with an error if the destination folder is
missing. Cloud services can also quietly remove empty folders, so leaving it in
does no harm.

This requires the GitHub setup from [guide 2](github-setup.qmd) to be finished,
because it authenticates as you.

::: {.callout-tip}
## In this course

Accepting an assignment on Classroom 50 creates a private repository named like
`gph-gu-2182-fall-2026-weekly-exercise-01-yourusername` inside the `gph-2182`
organization. So the one-liner is:

```r
dir.create("~/gph2182", showWarnings = FALSE)
usethis::create_from_github(
  "gph-2182/gph-gu-2182-fall-2026-weekly-exercise-01-yourusername",
  destdir = "~/gph2182"
)
```

with your own username on the end.
:::

## Situation B: you are starting something new

You have an idea, or an analysis, and nothing exists yet. Build it locally, then
publish it:

```r
usethis::create_project("~/gph2182/my-analysis")   # new project, opens in RStudio
usethis::use_git()                                 # make it a Git repository
usethis::use_github()                              # create it on GitHub and push
```

`use_git()` will offer to commit the existing files and to restart RStudio: say
yes to both. `use_github()` creates the remote repository under your account and
pushes your first commit, so the project exists on github.com when it finishes.

The menu equivalent of the first line is **File > New Project > New Directory >
New Project**.

## Situation C: opening a project you already have

**File > Recent Projects**, or double-click the `.Rproj` file in the folder. The
project name is always shown in the top-right corner of the RStudio window, so
you can tell at a glance which one you have open.

## Did it work?

Three checks, in order of usefulness:

1. **A Git tab** appears in the top-right pane, beside Environment and History.
   If it is missing, that is the whole problem: see
   [No Git tab](troubleshooting.qmd#no-git-tab).
2. **The project name** shows in the top-right corner of the window, not
   "Project: (None)".
3. **`getwd()`** in the Console prints the project folder.

## Working inside a project

- Write paths relative to the project root: `"data/raw.csv"`, not
  `"/Users/you/Desktop/data/raw.csv"`. The second one only works on your
  computer.
- Keep a shape that others can read: `data/` for inputs, `R/` for scripts,
  `figures/` for output.
- If you need to build paths from subfolders robustly, `here::here("data", "raw.csv")`
  resolves them from the project root no matter where the calling file lives.
- Do not put your token, passwords, or API keys in project files. They will be
  committed and pushed along with everything else.
